title: Needs-Based Selling: Sales Guide for Small Businesses
summary: Needs-based selling involves learning about your customers’ requirements and providing a tailored solution. Learn how to implement this sales strategy.
body_markdown:
Needs-based selling is a sales strategy built around the needs of the customer. Rather than leading with a product’s attributes, sales professionals using a needs-based approach consider how a given product is uniquely qualified to solve something in a customer’s life.


A[2026 HubSpot survey](https://www.hubspot.com/state-of-marketing) found that 93% of marketers said that personalization increases leads and purchases—but that only 16% knew their customers’ pain points and challenges. With customer-centric companies far outperforming their product-focused peers, it’s a meaningful gap that can be closed by putting customers’ needs first.


In this article, you’ll learn how to build a needs-based sales strategy, along with insights from successful businesses on what to prioritize


## What is needs-based selling?


Needs-based selling, also called consultative selling or a consultative approach, is a customer-centric sales strategy. Instead of leading with the qualities of a product, sales teams learn about the needs of the customer and then position their brand’s products as providing a solution.


Needs-based selling is often employed by sales teams for business-to-business (B2B) sales. Sales reps contact prospective clients and learn about their requirements, and then pitch one of their products or services as a solution. These may be tailored to the client’s specifications, budgets, and requirements. Direct to consumer (DTC) can employ similar strategies—gathering customer feedback and creating marketing and narratives based on what customers want.


### Needs-based selling vs. transactional selling vs. product-led selling


While needs-based sales, transactional sales, and product-led sales technically have the same goal—purchases—they use different tactics to get there.


Transaction-based selling prioritizes convenience and pricing as levers to gain customers—often for one-off transactions that don’t seek to build loyalty. Brands may offer one-off discounts, fast shipping, or other short-term incentives to make a sale, rather than build a relationship with the customer.


A product-led sale focuses on the features of a given product—detailing specs and function in sales pitches and marketing copy. Sales cycles may start with a free trial period to give customers an opportunity to engage with the product before completing the sale or interfacing with a salesperson.


A needs-based selling process prioritizes relationship-building over the course of a longer sales cycle, in order to position products as tailored solutions to pain points. The first step of this strategy is the discovery process; in a B2B setting, this may involve a sales rep taking time to build rapport and develop a nuanced understanding of their potential customers’ unique challenges before customizing their pitch accordingly.


In a direct-to-consumer setting, an example of this process might be extensive customer interviews during product development, or using interactive quizzes to give personal product recommendations based on customers’ needs.

## How to implement a needs-based selling strategy


1. Talk to your audience
2. Create templates for in-depth conversations
3. Build rich customer profiles
4. Personalize marketing campaigns
5. Create solutions-based narratives


Needs-based selling has three main stages: discovering a customer’s needs, evaluating how to meet them, and finally, making product recommendations based on the prior two. The discovery phase will require the most legwork, but it provides the foundation of a successful strategy.


“You have to do unscalable things to earn the right to find scalable solutions,"[Hearth Display](https://hearthdisplay.com/) ’s Susie Harrison says on an episode of the[Shopify Masters podcast](https://www.shopify.com/blog/hearth-display-pre-launch) . She and her cofounder each spent hours on the phone one-on-one with early customers, unearthing pain points and contextual details to guarantee their product, a digital wall calendar, could meet those needs. “We knew everything about those first customers, because it was so important to develop genuine relationships to see what that problem was—and what the solution would look like.”


While the early days may feel unscalable, there are ways to systematize each step of a customer-centric approach. Here’s how to build a needs-based sales strategy, step-by-step:


### Talk to your audience


The “needs” piece of a needs-based sales approach doesn’t have to be a mystery: start by talking to your prospective customers directly to find out what they’re looking for. That could include interviews with members of your target audience, livestreams or AMAs on your brand’s social media accounts, or in-store conversations—whether in your own retail location or in the aisles of a store where you hope your products will eventually be.


In a B2B setting, where needs-based[solution selling](https://www.shopify.com/blog/solution-selling?term=social%20selling&adid=565729637700&campaignid=15436644379&utm_medium=cpc&utm_source=google&matchtype=b&network=g&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=15436644379&gbraid=0AAAAADp4t0rSAMwig5vBhvAtR3IAULyr8&gclid=Cj0KCQjwzY7VBhDwARIsAFtPvBSAMCZfMvIfOGSn4hEJImsiOwqUTwG01Sn7gO9Nt_Tqg3YJLlCw1sEaAgJNEALw_wcB) is a common path to revenue growth and customer satisfaction, discovery is the initial phase of the sales cycle: long before sales reps pitch their company’s value proposition, they aim to cultivate a deep understanding of the prospective customer’s business and challenges.


[Hedley & Bennett](https://www.hedleyandbennett.com/) Founder Ellen Bennett credits her early conversations with chefs as accidental “focus grouping” that led to a line of products that seemed custom-made for their audience—because they were. “They gave me all the answers and the building blocks to create this company,” she says on *[Shopify Masters](https://www.shopify.com/blog/hedley-and-bennett-scaling-through-product-development-with-customers)* . “I got it right because I didn’t do it alone.”


### Create templates for in-depth conversation


“Lots of people think selling is about going in and giving a pitch about how great your product is,” Gloria Hwang, founder of helmet brand[Thousand](https://www.explorethousand.com/) , says on[Shopify Masters](https://www.shopify.com/blog/thousand-designing-for-safety) . “To me, the first 15 minutes of a pitch really should just be trying to understand what the person’s problems are and what you can potentially solve.”


There are many frameworks that sales teams use to shape those initial conversations and organize their findings, like[SPIN](https://www.shopify.com/blog/spin-selling) (situation, problem, implication, need-payoff), BANT (budget, authority, need, timing), or more extensive versions like MEDDIC (metrics, economic buyer, decision process, decision criteria, identified pain, and champion). Whichever you resonate with best, use it to create a lightly structured script with relevant questions for sales teams to adapt with their own words for[customer interviews](https://www.shopify.com/partners/blog/user-interview) . Leave room for follow-up questions based on the answers received.


Many sales professionals use the[Sandler Pain Funnel (](https://www.shopify.com/blog/pain-funnel) a systematic series of open-ended questions designed to identify and investigate a prospect’s pain points, then tie them to the cost implications and emotional impact of the issue) to understand an opportunity from as many angles as possible—and use them as support touchpoints for the product pitch that comes later.


Such in-depth interactions aren’t usually part of DTC sales, but ecommerce brands can still learn about customers’ needs and recommend products accordingly. For example, you can:


-


Equip your website with live chat functionality (as seen in[Shopify Inbox)](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/inbox/index) so you can gather context about a customer’s needs in real time, and ask questions that lead to best-fit, personalized product recommendations and links.


-


Design an[interactive quiz](https://www.shopify.com/blog/interactive-content#6-types-of-interactive-content) or quick survey on your homepage to help direct customers to personalized solutions. These interactive elements also gather useful data about individual customers that you can refer back to as you build out customer profiles.


### Build rich customer profiles


A[customer profile](https://www.shopify.com/blog/customer-profiling) is where all of the qualitative information you uncover during customer interviews meets demographics, contact info, purchase history, site activity, browsing paths, and historical engagement, so you can tailor the overall customer experience for maximum impact.


Use a[customer relationship management (CRM) platform](https://www.shopify.com/blog/crm-integration) to store customer data and communications, track where they are in the sales funnel and who is responsible for the next steps.


### Personalize marketing campaigns


Once you have robust customer profiles to work with, use them to build needs-driven marketing campaigns and personalized touchpoints.[Needs-based customer segmentation](https://www.shopify.com/blog/needs-based-segmentation) and[marketing automation tools](https://www.shopify.com/marketing-automation-tools) make it easy to group buyers by shared characteristics or behaviors, enabling data-driven[marketing outreach](https://www.shopify.com/blog/data-driven-marketing) and personalized follow-ups for cart abandonment, product recommendations, purchases, and more.


Common examples of[personalized marketing](https://www.shopify.com/enterprise/blog/63971715-how-to-maintain-a-personal-touch-with-customers-as-you-grow#6) include using a customer’s name in communications or tapping past purchases to inform recommendations. Marketing to the needs of separate customer segments is a more extensive approach. Say, for example, you sell electric cargo bikes and know you have two distinct audiences—parents looking for an eco-friendly, safe alternative to get their families around town, and young professionals looking for faster, cheaper commute options in a city. The marketing content you create for and send to each group will emphasize how your product can solve the problem relevant to them.


### Create solutions-based narratives


[Brand storytelling](https://www.shopify.com/blog/brand-storytelling) is a key pillar of needs-based selling. Once you know your customers’ needs, you can build narratives that speak to providing solutions for them. Copywriting frameworks, such as “features, advantages, and benefits (FAB)” or “[problem, agitation, solution (PAS)](https://www.shopify.com/blog/how-to-make-your-product-copy-more-persuasive) ,” can help you position your product in different scenarios.


For Dan Demsky, founder of[Unbound Merino](https://unboundmerino.com/) , focusing on providing solutions helped to differentiate the brand’s wool blend T-shirts in a crowded marketplace through its early motto: “Pack less, experience more.”


“That is always the primary focus of our messaging or marketing,” Dan says on *[Shopify Masters](https://www.shopify.com/blog/unbound-merino-scaling-to-one-hundred-million-lifetime-revenue)* . “We’re not a fashion brand, \[we’re\] a tool. I want to have nice clothing, but I don’t need to be on-trend. I don’t need to know what’s happening in fashion. I just want a great T-shirt that’s made of the best material, with the best fit. It serves the purpose that I need.”


A need for uncomplicated essentials led to brand storytelling that reflected the same principles: concise, direct copywriting that makes its points with clean style and efficiency. Take stock of your own storytelling approach, and find as many opportunities as you can to frame your offering from the customer’s point of view.


## Needs-based selling FAQ


### What is needs-based selling?


Needs-based selling is a customer-centric sales process that involves learning about customers’ needs and then positioning one’s products or services as providing the solution.


### What are the basic stages of needs-based selling?


The basic stages of needs-based selling are: fact-finding through customer research and conversation; evaluation of needs; and product recommendation.


### What is an example of needs-based selling?


An example of needs-based selling is a sales rep for employee recognition software learning about a company’s needs for such a tool. The sales rep asks questions about current company culture and processes, budget implications of not addressing the problem (high turnover), and hoped-for outcomes of employee engagement. They then recommend a tier of their software for the company, explaining how functionality can be tailored to meet their needs exactly.
